title: Downward-Facing Drones?
content: Through most of my professional career, I’ve had a tendency to examine all kinds of human pursuits through an entomological lens—that is to say, irrespective of the nature of the human pursuit, I inevitably find myself focusing on any connection, real or imagined, to insects. Thus, it’s not altogether surprising that what little I know about the practice of yoga relates to the handful of poses that are named for insects. To be clear, I have vanishingly little first-hand knowledge of yoga. The closest I get to yoga is occasionally purchasing boxes of YogiTea, a company founded in 1984 by Harbhajan Singh Khalsa (also known as Yogi Bhajan), a yoga guru and entrepreneur who died in 2004. YogiTea has been in the business of making “functional teas inspired by the ancient holistic philosophy of Ayurveda” for five decades (YogiTea 2024a). I did know that yoga poses can be named for animals, with downward-facing dog (adho mukha shvanasana) earning a special place in popular culture. Based on their names, some of these poses at first glance seem terrifying—for example, the cat-cow pose (chakravakasana), which, fortunately, appears to be an exercise involving switching between a cat pose and cow pose and not a pose based on some freakish bovine-feline hybrid (YogiTea 2024b).
